items.passage: Studies of how cephalopods camouflage themselves against the seafloor have concentrated on cuttlefish and octopuses, which typically rest on the bottom. Oval squid, by contrast, are semi-pelagic, inhabiting mostly the open water above it. Nevertheless, when Ryuta Nakajima and colleagues kept oval squid from Okinawa, Japan, in tanks, the animals adjusted the pigment cells in their skin to correspond to the substrate beneath them, modifying their patterning whenever they moved over a bottom of different reflectivity, a capacity never previously documented in the laboratory for any squid in their family.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research has shown that oval squid match their skin to the seafloor more rapidly than cuttlefish and octopuses do.
Research indicates that oval squid, though they rarely rest on the seafloor, can change their coloring to match it.
Researchers have found that oval squid in Okinawa change their skin patterns mainly to communicate in open water.
Because oval squid spend little time near the seafloor, they lack the pigment cells needed to match it.
items.explanation: The text contrasts cuttlefish and octopuses, which “typically rest on the bottom,” with oval squid, which inhabit “mostly the open water above it.” Even so, in tanks the squid “adjusted the pigment cells in their skin to correspond to the substrate beneath them.” The main idea is that oval squid, despite their open-water habits, can match the seafloor.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares how quickly oval squid, cuttlefish, and octopuses change color.

C.why_wrong: The squid changed their patterning in response to the bottom beneath them; the text says nothing about using color to communicate.

D.why_wrong: The squid “adjusted the pigment cells in their skin,” so they do have pigment cells that let them match the seafloor.

sources.what: Nakajima, Lajbner, Kuba et al. 2022, Scientific Reports: camouflage-to-substrate studies have focused on benthic cuttlefish and octopus; oval squid (Sepioteuthis lessoniana species complex) are semi-pelagic; in captivity S. lessoniana Sp. 2 from Okinawa adapts chromatophore coloration to the background substrate and changes patterning when moving between substrates of different reflectivity; not reported before in any loliginid under laboratory conditions

items.notes: Natural science (marine biology). Study report with a contrast (benthic vs semi-pelagic); key generalizes the finding. Ryuta Nakajima is the first author. Overlap check: no live item on cephalopod background matching (the squid items are vampire, bobtail, firefly and giant squid).

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (semi-pelagic oval squid from Okinawa match substrate in captivity; not reported before for any loliginid in the lab).

items.passage: The sculptor known as the Master of Rimini carved large numbers of alabaster figures around 1420 to 1440, and art historians have generally placed his workshop in Flanders or northern France, chiefly because his sculptures resemble Flemish and French paintings. When Wolfram Kloppmann and colleagues measured isotopes in the stone of works attributed to the master and his workshop, however, they found that all were carved from alabaster quarried in Franconia, in present-day northern Bavaria, some 600 kilometers away. The researchers therefore propose that the workshop operated in southern Germany.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have shown that the Master of Rimini learned to carve alabaster from sculptors who were working in Franconia.
The resemblance between the Master of Rimini’s sculptures and Flemish paintings shows that he was trained in the Low Countries.
Analysis of the stone in the Master of Rimini’s sculptures has led researchers to place his workshop in Germany, not Flanders or France.
Because alabaster was traded widely across medieval Europe, the source of a sculpture’s stone reveals little about where the sculpture was actually carved.
items.explanation: Art historians placed the workshop “in Flanders or northern France” because of the sculptures’ style, but Kloppmann and colleagues found that all the works were “carved from alabaster quarried in Franconia,” far from that region, and so “propose that the workshop operated in southern Germany.” The main idea is that the stone has led researchers to place the workshop in Germany instead.

A.why_wrong: The text says that the alabaster came from Franconia, not that the master learned his craft from sculptors there.

B.recipe: overstated (old evidence pushed to a conclusion)
B.why_wrong: The text says only that the resemblance led historians to place the workshop in Flanders or France; it never says that he trained in the Low Countries.

D.why_wrong: The researchers used the source of the stone to propose where the workshop was, so they treat it as revealing a great deal.

sources.what: Kloppmann et al. 2022, PLoS ONE: isotope fingerprints (Sr, S, O) of works attributed to the Master of Rimini (active about 1420 to 1440) and his workshop are virtually identical; material exclusively Franconian (northern Bavarian) alabaster, 600 km from the supposed Flemish or northern French workshop, whose location rested on similarities with Flemish and French painting; researchers propose a workshop in southern Germany

items.notes: Arts and humanities (art history). The key carries both halves (old placement and the revision), at medium length. The paper also suggests that the master may have trained in the Low Countries; the passage leaves this out, so B overreaches from the stylistic evidence the passage gives.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (Franconian alabaster 600 km away; prevailing Flemish or N-French attribution rests on painting parallels; southern German workshop proposed).

items.passage: The Libri Picturati, a collection of plant illustrations produced in the seventeenth-century Dutch colony in Brazil and now preserved in a library in Kraków, Poland, has primarily been studied for its artistic qualities. Mireia Alcàntara-Rodríguez and colleagues instead identified the plants depicted, which comprise 198 taxa, predominantly wild trees native to the rainforest. The illustrations also contain the earliest known record in Brazil of the Ethiopian pepper, a tree native to Africa.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can be concluded about the Ethiopian pepper?
options: It was present in Brazil by the 1600s despite originating elsewhere.
It was among the most widespread plants growing in the Dutch colony in Brazil at the time.
It was painted more often than any of the native rainforest trees in the collection.
It was first described as a distinct species by Alcàntara-Rodríguez and colleagues.
items.explanation: The text says that the illustrations were “produced in the seventeenth-century Dutch colony in Brazil” and that they contain “the earliest known record in Brazil of the Ethiopian pepper, a tree native to Africa.” So the plant had reached Brazil by the 1600s, though it came from elsewhere.

B.why_wrong: The text says that the Ethiopian pepper appears in the illustrations, not that it was common in the colony.

C.why_wrong: The 198 taxa are “predominantly wild trees native to the rainforest”; nothing says that the Ethiopian pepper was painted more often than any of them.

D.why_wrong: Alcàntara-Rodríguez and colleagues identified the plants in the illustrations; the text never says that they were the first to describe any species.

Ethiopian pepper (Xylopia aethiopica) is native to tropical Africa

items.notes: Arts and humanities with natural science (history of botany). One-step inference, as in 2.19: painted in the colony in the 1600s plus native to Africa, so present in Brazil by then though not native. The paper also names the sunflower; left out (another item in this batch is about sunflower pollen). items.passage: In the 1960s, British artist Tom Phillips came across a forgotten Victorian novel, William Hurrell Mallock’s A Human Document, and began painting, drawing, and collaging over its pages, leaving only scattered fragments of the original text visible. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Phillips set out to rescue a forgotten Victorian novel by drawing new readers to Mallock’s original story.
Phillips’s A Humument is admired mainly for the images that cover its pages rather than for its story.
Over the decades, Phillips’s pages have grown steadily less abstract as he has allowed more of Mallock’s original words to show through.
Phillips created a new story by covering most of an existing novel’s text and keeping only some of its words.
items.explanation: Phillips painted and collaged over the pages of “a forgotten Victorian novel,” “leaving only scattered fragments of the original text visible,” and those words “constitute an entirely new narrative about a character named Bill Toge.” The main idea is that he made a new work and a new story out of an existing book.

A.recipe: twisted detail (example turned into a purpose)
A.why_wrong: Phillips covered most of Mallock’s words to tell a new story; the text never says that he wanted readers to read Mallock’s novel.

B.why_wrong: The text never says how A Humument is received or which part of it is most admired.

C.recipe: chronological story the text does not tell

Mallock’s 1892 novel A Human Document, begun in the 1960s, first edition 1970, completed 2016; Phillips drew, painted and collaged over the pages leaving some original text visible; new story with protagonist Bill Toge, whose name appears only where together or altogether appears; later editions revise and replace pages

items.notes: Arts and humanities (visual art, artist's book). Profile: aim and method, one concrete detail (Bill Toge), effect. Key generalizes the method; distractors follow the T3 recipes (example as purpose, invented reputation, invented chronology).

The following text is adapted from Winifred Holtby’s 1924 novel The Crowded Street. Eleven-year-old Muriel has come to a children’s dance with her mother, Mrs. Hammond.

“It’s nearly time to begin dancing,” said Muriel’s mother. “We must get your programme filled. There are a lot of little boys here whom you know. Look, there’s Freddy Mason. You remember him, dear, don’t you?”

“I don’t think—” she began in her prim little voice. She was about to add—“that I want to dance with Freddy,” when Mrs. Hammond finished her sentence for her.

“Of course he’ll want to dance with you, dear.” Mrs. Hammond claimed that she knew what went on in Muriel’s mind—her own child’s mind. She often finished Muriel’s hesitating sentences for her. “You mustn’t be so shy, dear,” she reproved gently.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Muriel is too shy to speak to Freddy, so her mother kindly steps in and introduces the two children to each other.
Muriel and her mother argue about whether Freddy would be a suitable partner until Muriel gives in.
Muriel’s mother, sure that she knows her daughter’s thoughts, answers for Muriel and overlooks the girl’s actual wishes.
Mrs. Hammond gently scolds Muriel for having been rude to Freddy the last time they met.
items.explanation: Muriel starts to say that she does not want to dance with Freddy, but Mrs. Hammond “finished her sentence for her” with the opposite meaning. The text explains that Mrs. Hammond “claimed that she knew what went on in Muriel’s mind” and “often finished Muriel’s hesitating sentences.” So the main idea is that the mother, sure she knows Muriel’s thoughts, speaks for her and misses her real wish.

A.why_wrong: Mrs. Hammond calls Muriel shy, but Muriel is trying to say that she does not want to dance with Freddy; the mother overrides her rather than helping her.

B.why_wrong: There is no argument: Muriel never finishes her sentence, and her mother does not realize that Muriel objects.

D.why_wrong: Mrs. Hammond “reproved gently” for shyness, not for rudeness, and the text never mentions Muriel being rude to Freddy.

sources.what: Winifred Holtby, The Crowded Street (1924), prologue, Project Gutenberg text

items.notes: Literary prose. Excerpt copied exactly with one paragraph trimmed between the first and second paragraphs (Muriel's memory of a frightening fall from a haystack while playing with Freddy, ending “But she did not now want to dance with Freddy”); Gutenberg's double and quadruple hyphens set as closed em dashes and quotes made curly. review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 68629 (one paragraph trimmed); Muriel is eleven in the prologue.

items.passage: The cemetery of Jebel Sahaba, in the Nile Valley of northern Sudan, holds the remains of 61 people buried at least 13,400 years ago, many of them bearing injuries inflicted by weapons. Since the site was excavated in the 1960s, it has often been interpreted as the record of a single conflict. However, when Isabelle Crevecoeur and colleagues reexamined the skeletons microscopically, they identified more than 100 previously undocumented injuries, and a quarter of the individuals with injuries had both healed and unhealed wounds.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have confirmed that most of the people buried at Jebel Sahaba died in a single conflict, as the original excavators had proposed.
A reexamination of the Jebel Sahaba skeletons suggests that the people buried there faced repeated violence, not a single conflict.
Crevecoeur and colleagues found that the injuries at Jebel Sahaba were caused by different weapons than earlier researchers had believed.
Because many of the injuries at Jebel Sahaba had healed, researchers now doubt that the site records any violence at all.
items.explanation: The site “has often been interpreted as the record of a single conflict,” but the reexamination found that “a quarter of the individuals with injuries had both healed and unhealed wounds.” People who survived earlier injuries and then received new ones were caught up in violence more than once, so the main idea is that the violence recurred rather than occurring in a single conflict.

A.recipe: contradicts the text (affirms the earlier view)
A.why_wrong: The healed and unhealed wounds point away from a single conflict, and the text presents the reexamination as challenging that view.

C.why_wrong: The text says that the injuries were “inflicted by weapons” but never discusses which weapons or compares the findings with earlier beliefs about them.

D.why_wrong: The reexamination found even more injuries than before, so it adds evidence of violence rather than casting doubt on it.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (over 100 new lesions, a quarter with healed and unhealed trauma, single warfare event dismissed).

items.passage: Many restaurants in Japan display their dishes, from bowls of ramen to plates of sushi, in the front window as replicas known as shokuhin sampuru. Why would restaurants spend so much on food that no one can eat? Unlike real dishes, the replicas can remain on display indefinitely without spoiling or attracting insects. How do artisans make shokuhin sampuru look so much like real food?
Which dishes are most often reproduced as shokuhin sampuru?
Why have some restaurants in Japan stopped displaying shokuhin sampuru?

B.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
B.why_wrong: The text says that the models are handcrafted from polyvinyl chloride, but it does not explain how they are made to look real.

C.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
C.why_wrong: Ramen and sushi are given as examples, but the text never says which dishes are reproduced most often.

D.recipe: on-topic question the text never takes up
D.why_wrong: The text never mentions restaurants that have stopped using the replicas.

People who bought her work kept asking for those subjects.
She wanted her paintings to match the flowers she had painted on her walls.

items.passage: In 1911, Cora Wilson Stewart, the superintendent of schools in Rowan County, Kentucky, established what she called Moonlight Schools, where adults who could not read attended evening classes in the same schoolhouses that children used during the day. No reading books existed that were suited to adults who were beginning to read.

items.passage: Every spring in Austria, common frogs leave the places where they spent the winter and travel to ponds to breed, and many are killed on roads along the way. Temporary protective measures can save them, but only if those measures are in place in time. Analyzing thousands of observations recorded by volunteers, Maria Peer and colleagues found that the frogs’ migration closely followed the flowering of certain plants, such as goat willow and apricot trees. The researchers suggest that such flowering could signal when protections should be set up.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that the flowering of certain plants could help people predict when common frogs will begin migrating.
Volunteers in Austria have built barriers that keep most common frogs from being killed on roads.
Common frogs decide when to migrate by watching for the blossoms of goat willow and apricot trees.
Researchers have shown that roads are the main cause of the decline of frogs in Austria.
items.explanation: Peer and colleagues “found that the frogs’ migration closely followed the flowering of certain plants,” and they “suggest that such flowering could signal when protections should be set up.” The main idea is that plant flowering could help predict when the frogs will migrate.

B.why_wrong: The text says that volunteers recorded observations and that temporary measures can save frogs, but it never says that volunteers built barriers that protect most frogs.

C.why_wrong: The migration “closely followed” the flowering; the text never says that the frogs watch for blossoms.

D.why_wrong: The text says that many frogs are killed on roads, not that roads are the main cause of a decline.

sources.what: Peer, Dörler, Zaller et al. 2021, Scientific Reports: roads disrupt amphibian migration between hibernation and breeding sites, causing roadkill; timely temporary mitigation measures needed; 3,751 amphibian and 7,818 plant phenology observations from Austrian citizen science; common frog migration closely associated with phenology of European larch, goat willow and apricot; plant phenology can be used to time temporary mitigation measures

items.notes: Natural science (ecology). Easy study report, main idea in the last sentence as in 1.8 and 1.10, key hedged with could to match suggest. The study also covered common toads (weaker association), left out.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract (Austrian citizen-science data; common frog migration closely tied to goat willow and apricot phenology; timing of temporary measures).

items.passage: Psychologist David Brieber and colleagues investigated whether the setting in which people encounter art affects how they respond to it. Two groups of participants viewed the artworks from an exhibition, one group in a museum and the other in a laboratory, while a mobile eye-tracking device recorded how long each person examined each work. Afterward, participants evaluated the works. Participants in the museum looked at the artworks longer, considered them more interesting, and liked them more than participants in the laboratory did.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that wearing eye-tracking devices causes people to spend less time looking at art.
Psychologists found that people prefer paintings to other kinds of art, whether in a museum or a laboratory.
A study showed that people enjoy art more when they view it with a group of friends than when they view it by themselves.
A study found that people respond more favorably to artworks when they see them in a museum than in a laboratory.
items.explanation: The researchers compared viewers “in a museum” with viewers “in a laboratory,” and participants in the museum “looked at the artworks longer, considered them more interesting, and liked them more.” So the main idea is that people respond more favorably to art seen in a museum.

A.why_wrong: Both groups wore the eye-tracking device, so the study could not show that the device itself shortened viewing time.

B.why_wrong: The text never compares paintings with other kinds of art.

C.why_wrong: The two groups saw the art in different places; the text never compares viewing in a group with viewing alone.

sources.what: Brieber, Nadal, Leder, Rosenberg 2014, PLoS ONE: two groups viewed an art exhibition, one in the museum and one in the laboratory, with viewing time recorded by a mobile eye tracking system; participants then rated the artworks; museum participants liked the artworks more, found them more interesting, and viewed them longer

items.notes: Social science (psychology of art). Easy study report like 1.11. Overlap note: a live Words in Context item uses the Met's average viewing time per artwork (Smith and Smith 2001); this item's premise is the museum versus laboratory comparison.

review.note: Core claim matches the abstract. Overlap judged: the live WiC item words_in_context.B5.medium.w2b1_07 is about how briefly Met visitors look at masterpieces; this premise is the museum-versus-laboratory context effect on liking, so it is a different claim, not a clone; kept.

items.passage:
The following text is from E. M. Delafield’s 1919 novel Consequences. Alex, the eldest of several children, has been explaining a new game to her siblings. Emily, the nursery-maid who is supervising them, has just praised her.

“Quite right, Miss Alex; what a clever girl, to be sure. Here, Master Baby, you can play with me. You’re too little to do it all by yourself.”

“He isn’t Baby any more. We’ve got to call him Archie now. The new little sister is Baby,” said Alex dictatorially.

She liked always to be the one to give information, and Emily had only been with them a little while.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Alex is embarrassed that Emily has praised her in front of the other children.
Alex is jealous that her little brother is getting so much of Emily’s attention.
Alex enjoys being the one who tells others how things are, even when the other person is an adult.
Alex is unsure what the family has decided to call the new baby.
items.explanation: When Emily calls the little boy “Master Baby,” Alex corrects her “dictatorially,” explaining that he is now Archie and that “The new little sister is Baby.” The narrator adds that Alex “liked always to be the one to give information.” So the main idea is that Alex enjoys telling others how things are, even an adult such as Emily.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Alex is embarrassed; she answers Emily’s praise by correcting her with confidence.

B.why_wrong: Alex speaks up when Emily addresses her brother, but the text explains her remark by her liking “to be the one to give information,” not by jealousy.

D.why_wrong: Alex states plainly, “The new little sister is Baby,” so she is not unsure.

sources.what: E. M. Delafield, Consequences (1919), chapter I, “The Game of Consequences,” Project Gutenberg text

items.notes: Literary prose. Three consecutive paragraphs copied exactly (Gutenberg's straight quotes made curly); the opening paragraphs, in which Alex explains the game, are summed up in the context line. Easy: the narrator states the trait outright, and the key restates it in plain terms.

review.note: Excerpt checked word for word against Gutenberg 34935.

items.passage: The Human Library, which began in Copenhagen, Denmark, in 2000, operates much like a conventional library, except that its “books” are people. Each “book” is someone who has experienced prejudice or exclusion, and visitors can “borrow” one for a conversation, asking questions they might never otherwise have the chance to ask. The organization’s goal is to help participants examine their own assumptions about others. The first event, held at Denmark’s Roskilde Festival, drew more than 1,000 participants, and the organization is now active in more than 85 countries.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The Human Library lends out books in which people who have faced prejudice describe their own lives in their own words.
The Human Library aims to challenge prejudice through conversations with people who have experienced it.
The Human Library started as a festival event and has since replaced traditional libraries in many countries.
The Human Library trains librarians to recommend books about prejudice to their visitors.
items.explanation: In the Human Library, the “books” are people who have “experienced prejudice or exclusion,” and visitors “borrow” them for conversations. The organization’s goal is “to help participants examine their own assumptions about others.” So the main idea is that the organization uses conversations to challenge prejudice.

A.recipe: twisted detail (the library analogy taken literally)
A.why_wrong: The text puts “books” in quotation marks because the books are people; visitors talk with them rather than reading written life stories.

C.why_wrong: The text says that the first event was held at a festival and that the organization is active in many countries, not that it has replaced traditional libraries.

D.why_wrong: The text never mentions librarians or recommending books.

sources.what: The Human Library, Wikipedia: began in Copenhagen in 2000 with the first event at the Roskilde Festival (more than 1,000 participants); aims to address prejudice by helping people talk to those they would not normally meet; lends people rather than books, people who have experienced prejudice, social exclusion or stigma; readers ask questions to challenge their own prejudices; active in over 85 countries

items.notes: Social science (civic organization). Profile: aim, method, example, reach; the key generalizes the method and aim. A takes the library analogy literally, C and D are the invented-reach and invented-method recipes.
